notes.text: Here we encounter yet another example of the idiocy of the lexicography of LS2. This word does not mean storm. It is rather the word ܥܪܡܘܬܐ that provides the semantics of a forceful storm while stwɁ simply tells us it is a winter one. The example in the "Bauer-Meissner papyrus" has not been generally recognized since it appears to have prefixed "d_" after the same word spelled "zy"; but the latter is of course a literary spelling of a form that had almost certainly already shifted to "d" in pronunciation, so we take the expression to be a fixed expression "wintery, late crop".

At Qumran there seems to be a clear difference between syp "physical end" and swp "chronological end", but that distinction does not hold elsewhere. Note the regular confusion in the Jewish texts over with the expression "to be full end-to-end" uses this word or the word sp "threshold". DJPA assumes that all examples of this form in Gal. are to be understood as errors for swp; thus so usually parsed in such texts, although we are not so certain.

notes.text: The interpretation is based on the appearance of this word in other rabbinic Hebrew texts related to this passage. See Jastrow and DJBA s.v. רצינתא. The scribe here apparently thought it was a verbal form, however, hence ולא instead of דלא. The etymology, though, (for which compare Levy and Jastrow), remains uncertain. The standard edition of the Talmud (BB 91b) reads: ת"ר ואכלתם מן התבואה ישן בלא סלמנטון מאי בלא סלמנטון רב נחמן אמר בלא רצינתא ורב ששת אמר בלא שדיפא : the sages taught: you shall eat from the old grain (Lev. 25:22) means without s’. What is "without s’?" PN1 said without רצינתא while PN2 said without blast.

notes.text: Müller-Kessler BSOAS 75(2012):21 proposes that this form is always due solely to orthographic confusion between /ṭ/ and /g/ in Mandaic script. It might be a compelling suggestion except for the facts that the parallel noun from that root (i.s. sṭm) appears as sidma in Mandaic and the root appears in JBAmb, where the graphic confusion would not occur. So we think rather that it is a legitimate lexical expansion from sqm vb. Alternatively (or additionally?) one might compare the Greek loans sgmwṭyn n.m. "covering" and/or zgmɁ n.m.pl. "bolt". citations.translation: (they walked) between mountains and valleys and hills and dales

notes.text: Bedjan vocalizes as if the same as #1, while LS2 points out that this is an Arabism and a different word; in the context it is clearly an area between low hills as opposed to a valley between mountains.
